lead: Static CMOS builds every gate from two complementary networks: a pMOS pull-up that connects the output to V<sub>DD</sub> and an nMOS pull-down that connects it to ground. In steady state one network is off, so the output reaches a rail and no direct path carries current. Ratioed logic removes part of that complement: an always-on load pulls up while an nMOS network pulls down. It saves transistors, but the low output sits above 0 V and the load draws static current whenever the output is low. These styles appear in dense gates, SRAM-like cells and older NMOS designs.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.1 for the inverter voltage transfer curve and Chapter 3.2 for pseudo-nMOS loads.

blocks.text: Static CMOS builds a gate from two complementary networks. The pMOS pull-up network connects the output to V<sub>DD</sub> when it is on. The nMOS pull-down network connects the output to ground when it is on. For every input combination, exactly one network conducts. In an inverter, a high input turns the nMOS on and the output is 0 V; a low input turns the pMOS on and the output is V<sub>DD</sub>. In a multi-input gate the pull-down conducts only when its own combination of inputs is satisfied, and the pull-up is then off. Some syllabi call this complementary CMOS.

Drawing rule: the pull-down network uses nMOS transistors and implements the logic function directly. The pull-up network uses pMOS transistors and is the dual: series branches become parallel, and parallel branches become series. An inverter needs 1 pMOS and 1 nMOS. A two-input NAND or NOR needs 4 transistors. A simple N-input gate needs 2N transistors.

Because one network is always off in steady state, there is no direct path from VDD to ground. The output reaches a rail: VOH = VDD and VOL = 0 V. Full swing gives large noise margins, as Chapter 3.1 explains. Static current is only leakage. The cost is transistor count and input capacitance: 2N transistors for N inputs, and the pMOS network is often widened to match nMOS drive.

Ratioed logic replaces the complementary pull-up with an always-on load. In pseudo-nMOS, the load is a pMOS transistor with its gate tied to 0 V. The pMOS is always on. The nMOS pull-down network still implements the logic. In a saturated nMOS load, the load is an nMOS transistor with its gate tied to V<sub>DD</sub>. Both are ratioed: the output low voltage depends on the ratio of the pull-down strength to the load strength.

When the output is high, the nMOS network is off. In pseudo-nMOS the pMOS load pulls the output all the way to V<sub>DD</sub>. In a saturated nMOS load the load turns off once its gate-source voltage falls to V<sub>tn</sub>, where V<sub>tn</sub> is the nMOS threshold voltage, so the output high is V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>. The swing is degraded at both ends. In either case no current flows except leakage. When the output is low, the nMOS network is on. The load and the driver both conduct, so a static current flows from V<sub>DD</sub> to ground. The output does not reach 0 V. The load and driver form a voltage divider, so V<sub>OL</sub> > 0 V.

blocks.where: I<sub>load</sub> is the pMOS saturation current in µA; k<sub>p</sub> = µ<sub>p</sub>C<sub>ox</sub>(W/L)<sub>p</sub> in µA/V²; V<sub>DD</sub> is the supply in V; |V<sub>tp</sub>| is the pMOS threshold magnitude in V. This holds when the pMOS is in saturation. The pMOS is in saturation when |V<sub>DS</sub>| ≥ |V<sub>GS</sub>| − |V<sub>tp</sub>|, that is V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub> ≥ V<sub>DD</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|, which needs V<sub>OL</sub> ≤ |V<sub>tp</sub>|. The static power is P<sub>static</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> × I<sub>load</sub> when the output is low. Pseudo-nMOS uses N+1 transistors for an N-input gate, not 2N. The saving in area is the reason it exists.

blocks.text: Table 1 compares the styles. Static CMOS has full swing, the best noise margin and almost no static current. Ratioed logic has fewer transistors and smaller area. It pays with V<sub>OL</sub> > 0 V, reduced low noise margin and static current when the output is low. The always-on pMOS is weak, so the low-to-high transition is slow; the nMOS driver is strong, so the high-to-low transition is fast. Use ratioed logic only where area matters more than static power, such as dense regular arrays and some SRAM-like cells.

Some syllabi group tristate and clocked CMOS here as short variants of static CMOS. A tristate inverter adds enable transistors in series with the pull-up and pull-down. When disabled, both paths are off and the output is high impedance. Clocked CMOS, often written C²MOS, puts clock transistors in series with the complementary networks. Both keep rail-to-rail outputs when enabled. They are not ratioed because they do not use an always-on load. Pass-transistor and dynamic styles are separate; see Chapter 3.8 and Chapter 3.9.

figure.caption: Static CMOS uses a complementary pull-up and pull-down; ratioed logic replaces the pull-up with an always-on load, so the output low is above 0 V.

spec.aria: A tree comparing complementary static CMOS with two ratioed loads: pseudo-nMOS and saturated nMOS load.

examples.question: A pseudo-nMOS inverter uses V<sub>DD</sub> = 2.5 V, k<sub>n</sub> = 100 µA/V², V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.5 V, k<sub>p</sub> = 20 µA/V² and |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.5 V. The pMOS gate is tied to 0 V and the nMOS input is at V<sub>DD</sub>. (a) Find the load current. (b) Find V<sub>OL</sub> and state whether the pMOS load is in saturation.
steps: The pMOS source is at V<sub>DD</sub> = 2.5 V and its gate is at 0 V, so |V<sub>GS</sub>| = 2.5 V. The overdrive is |V<sub>GS</sub>| − |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 2.0 V.
Assume the pMOS load is in saturation. I<sub>load</sub> = (20 µA/V² / 2)(2.0 V)² = 40 µA.
The nMOS driver has V<sub>GS</sub> = 2.5 V and V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>OL</sub>. Its overdrive is 2.0 V, so it is in the linear region for small V<sub>OL</sub>.
Set the driver linear current equal to the load current: 40 µA = 100 µA/V²[(2.0 V)V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>²/2].
Divide by 100 µA/V²: 0.4 = 2V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>²/2. Rearrange: V<sub>OL</sub>² − 4V<sub>OL</sub> + 0.8 = 0.
Solve: V<sub>OL</sub> = (4 − √12.8)/2 = (4 − 3.5777)/2 = 0.211 V. The other root, 3.789 V, is not physical.
Check pMOS saturation: |V<sub>DS</sub>| = 2.5 V − 0.211 V = 2.289 V, which is greater than 2.0 V. The assumption holds.
examples.answer: The load current is 40 µA and V<sub>OL</sub> ≈ 0.211 V; the pMOS load is in saturation.
examples.check:
VDD = 2.5
kn = 100.0
Vtn = 0.5
kp = 20.0
Vtp = 0.5
Iload = (kp / 2) * (VDD - Vtp) ** 2
a = kn / 2
b = -kn * (VDD - Vtn)
c = Iload
V = (-b - (b * b - 4 * a * c) ** 0.5) / (2 * a)
print(round(Iload, 1))
print(round(V, 3))

traps: Never say a ratioed gate has zero static power. The load conducts whenever the output is low, so P<sub>static</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> × I<sub>load</sub>.
Do not use the driver saturation equation when V<sub>OL</sub> is small. The driver is in the linear region because V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>OL</sub> is below V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>.
Do not confuse the transistor ratio W/L with the logic ratio. V<sub>OL</sub> is set by the strength ratio of pull-down to pull-up, not by transistor count alone.
Ratioed logic does not give full rail-to-rail swing. V<sub>OL</sub> > 0 V, so the low noise margin is smaller than in static CMOS.
Static CMOS has almost no static current in steady state, but it has short-circuit current during switching. That is dynamic power, not the always-on load current of ratioed logic.

quiz.q: What are the two networks in static CMOS, and which transistors form each?
quiz.a: A pMOS pull-up network to V<sub>DD</sub> and an nMOS pull-down network to ground. They are complementary: exactly one conducts for each input.

quiz.q: Why does static CMOS draw almost no static current in steady state?
quiz.a: A steady input turns one network off. There is no direct path from V<sub>DD</sub> to ground, so only leakage current flows.

quiz.q: A pseudo-nMOS inverter has k<sub>p</sub> = 40 µA/V², V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V, |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.4 V and the pMOS gate at 0 V. Find the load current.
quiz.a: |V<sub>GS</sub>| − |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 1.8 V − 0.4 V = 1.4 V. I<sub>load</sub> = (40 µA/V² / 2)(1.4 V)² = 20 × 1.96 µA = 39.2 µA.

quiz.q: Explain why V<sub>OL</sub> > 0 V in ratioed logic and what it does to the low noise margin.
quiz.a: The always-on load and the conducting pull-down form a voltage divider, so the output low settles above 0 V. A higher V<sub>OL</sub> reduces the low noise margin NM<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>IL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>.

quiz.q: For the worked example, find the static power when the output is low.
quiz.a: P<sub>static</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> × I<sub>load</sub> = 2.5 V × 40 µA = 100 µW.

quiz.q: A designer replaces a static CMOS NAND with pseudo-nMOS to save area. Give one benefit and two costs.
quiz.a: Benefit: an N-input gate uses N+1 transistors instead of 2N. Costs: static current while the output is low, a raised (degraded) V<sub>OL</sub> above 0 V with reduced low noise margin, and a slower low-to-high transition because the pMOS load is weak.
A static CMOS inverter with enable transistors in series with the pull-up and pull-down. When disabled, both paths are off and the output is high impedance.

beyond: Not for the exam. Ratioed logic survives in SRAM bit cells and some sense amplifiers, where a small cell area matters more than a continuous current. Static CMOS remains the default in standard-cell libraries because full swing and near-zero static power scale well with supply voltage. FinFET and multi-V<sub>t</sub> processes make the ratioed trade-off sharper: lower V<sub>DD</sub> reduces static power but also reduces noise margin. Search next for pseudo-nMOS ratio design, complementary CMOS sizing, and C²MOS clocked logic.
